questions.stem: A 60-kg man (body fluid osmolality 290 mOsm/kg; 60-40-20 rule) has 360 mmol of NaCl added to his ECF. NaCl stays in the ECF. What is his new body fluid osmolality?
questions.explanation: TBW 36 L; total osmoles 36 × 290 = 10,440. NaCl adds 720 mOsm (2 osmoles per mole) → 11,160/36 = 310 mOsm/kg. Water shifts ICF → ECF until both are equal (ICF ≈ 22.5 L, ECF ≈ 13.5 L). A: NaCl is an effective osmole and raises osmolality. B: Counts NaCl as 1 osmole. D: Counts 1 osmole and ignores the water shift (ECF 12 L only). E: Ignores the water shift from the ICF.

questions.stem: A 70-kg man (osmolality 290 mOsm/kg; 60-40-20 rule) rapidly drinks 3 L of water. After full absorption but before any excretion, what is his plasma osmolality?
questions.explanation: Total osmoles 42 × 290 = 12,180; new TBW 45 L → 271 mOsm/kg in all compartments (ICF 30 L, ECF 15 L; water splits 2/3 : 1/3). A: Water dilutes all compartments. C: Keeps all 3 L in the ECF (4060/17). D: Subtracts the water instead of adding it. E: Puts all 3 L into the ICF (8120/31).

questions.stem: Red cells are placed in 300 mM urea. What happens?

options.A: They swell, because urea enters and water follows
options.B: They shrink, because urea draws water out
options.C: No change, because the solution is isosmotic
options.D: No change, because urea is an impermeant solute
options.E: They shrink, then return to normal volume

questions.explanation: 300 mM urea is isosmotic but hypotonic: urea is permeant, equilibrates across the membrane, and exerts no effective osmotic force, so water enters and cells swell (may burst). B: Urea isn't an effective osmole. C: Isosmotic doesn't mean isotonic. D: Urea is permeant. E: There is no initial shrinkage in the lecture's model.

questions.stem: Which IV fluid is approximately isosmotic in the bag, yet expands both ECF and ICF after infusion?
questions.explanation: D5W (~252 mOsm/L) is near-isosmotic, but glucose is metabolized, leaving free water that distributes into ECF and ICF. A: Isotonic saline stays in the ECF. B: 0.45% NaCl also expands both, but it is hyposmotic in the bag (~154 mOsm/L). D: Mannitol is hyperosmotic and shrinks the ICF. E: Lactated Ringer's is clinically isotonic and stays in the ECF.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with a severe head injury has rising intracranial pressure. IV mannitol is given. Which change explains its immediate effect?

options.A: It enters neurons and raises their osmolality
options.B: It lowers plasma osmolality, so water leaves the brain
options.C: It raises plasma oncotic pressure like albumin
options.D: It crosses the blood–brain barrier and pulls water into the CSF
options.E: It raises plasma osmolality, drawing water out of brain tissue

questions.explanation: Mannitol is poorly permeable, an effective extracellular osmole: it raises plasma osmolality and draws water from brain cells and interstitium (if the BBB is intact), then causes osmotic diuresis. A: It stays extracellular. B: It raises, not lowers, plasma osmolality. C: It is a sugar alcohol, not a protein. D: It works only if the BBB keeps it out.

questions.stem: Which statement about tonicity is correct?

options.A: 150 mM NaCl and 300 mM urea are both isotonic
options.B: Tonicity includes all solutes, permeant or not
options.C: Infused glucose has a sustained osmotic effect in healthy people
options.D: Tonicity depends only on impermeant solutes
options.E: Isosmotic solutions never change cell volume

questions.explanation: Only impermeant (effective) solutes set tonicity. A: The urea solution is hypotonic. B: That describes osmolarity. C: Rapidly metabolized solutes like dextrose have no sustained osmotic effect. E: Isosmotic urea swells cells.

questions.stem: A 70-kg man (osmolality 290 mOsm/kg) receives 2 L of isotonic saline. What are his final ECF and ICF volumes?
questions.explanation: Isotonic saline doesn't change effective ECF osmolality, so no water shifts: all 2 L stay in the ECF (14 → 16 L) and the ICF stays 28 L. B: Splits the saline 1/3 : 2/3 as if it were water. C: Results of adding NaCl alone (water shifts out of cells). D: Water doesn't leave the ICF. E: Puts all the fluid in the cells.

questions.stem: A patient with nephrotic syndrome is losing protein in the urine and develops generalized edema. Which mechanism is primary?
questions.explanation: Loss of plasma protein leaves less oncotic pressure to pull fluid back into capillaries (hypoalbuminemia; kidney or liver disease). A: Raised hydrostatic pressure is heart failure or venous obstruction. C: Increased permeability is inflammation or burns. D: Lymphatic obstruction is node removal or filariasis. E: Plasma osmolality (crystalloid) doesn't drive edema across capillaries; proteins do.
